title: Farid: the Creator in creation
hookLine: the Creator lives in creation and creation in the Creator, so whom can we call bad (Farid salok, ang 1381)
tomorrow: Farid: the crows and the eyes

lines: THAT WAS A BAD THING TO DO.
cards: Anyone who's spent time around small children has heard the rule, or used it. Not: you're a bad boy. Instead: that was a bad thing to do.
Teachers and parents swear by it, because a child who keeps hearing he is bad starts to believe it.

Grown-ups break that rule about each other all day, mostly in their heads: that coworker is useless, that cousin is impossible. And once someone's filed under bad, you stop seeing anything else in them.
Sheikh Farid, the Sufi of Pakpattan, asked a question that makes that filing system very hard to keep running.

teach.b: On Ang 1381 comes this salok: fareedaa khaalak khalak mahi khalak vasai rab maahi; mandaa kis no aakheeai jaa tis bin koee naahi. Farid, the Creator is in the creation, and the creation lives in God.
Whom, then, can we call bad, when there's no one without Him? The first half should sound familiar.
Six days ago, Kabir's hymn on Ang 1349 used the same pair of Arabic words: khaalik, the Creator, and khalak, the creation, each folded into the other. So it isn't a new idea; it's an older voice.

Farid lived in the thirteenth century, about two hundred years before Kabir, and the Gurus kept both in one book. But Farid's question is narrower, and sharper. Kabir asked who is good and who is bad.

teach.h: AAKHEEAI — WHOM SHALL WE CALL BAD.
teach.b: Farid's verb is aakheeai, to call, to say out loud: not who is bad, but whom shall we call bad. It's a question about the tongue, the label hung on someone.

You heard the same two words, mandaa and aakheeai, on day 247, when Guru Nanak asked why woman should be called lesser. Each time, the question turns back on the one doing the calling. Careful, though.
Farid isn't saying nothing is ever wrong; his saloks are full of warnings about wasted lives and cruel deeds.

teach.h: NAME THE DEED, NOT THE PERSON.
teach.b: You can name a wrong act clearly.
What he questions is the word stamped on the whole person: bad, done, filed. That label fits no one, because there's no one without God in them. So the file never quite closes.

how: Farid's salok on the Creator in creation is widely quoted by Sikhs, often with Kabir's 'from one light', to speak of seeing God in every person.

o: the Sikh Guru who wrote of the Creator
Kabir's teacher, who gave him that word pair
the Sufi who asked whom we can call bad

games.q: inside Farid's salok — tap the pairs.
p: to call, to say out loud

s: Farid says nothing anyone does is ever wrong
his saloks warn about cruel deeds; he questions the verdict on the whole person.
Farid learned this pair of words from Kabir
Farid lived about two hundred years before Kabir; the Gurus kept both voices in one book.
khaalik and khalak are Arabic words
the Creator and the creation, almost the same word.

games.q: someone at work has done something genuinely wrong. how does Farid's salok help?
o: call them bad and be done with them.
name the wrong deed clearly, but don't write off the person, since God lives in them too.
games.why: mandaa kis no aakheeai jaa tis bin koee naahi: no one is without God, so the verdict on the person stays open.

practice: Hold in mind one person you've quietly filed under bad, without pretending they've done nothing wrong. Set Farid's question beside them: the Creator lives in them too, so whom shall I call bad?
If nothing shifts, that's fine; just breathe with the question and let it stay open.

wordCard.voice: Farid. Here, his salok: the Creator is in the creation and the creation in God, so whom can we call bad, when no one is without Him?

orig.note: Gurmukhi: khaalik, the Creator; from Arabic, set beside khalak, the creation.

carryVoice: Your line: whom shall I call bad. The deed can be named; the person stays open. See you tomorrow.
